steps.say: Catheterisation remains the reference standard when echo leaves questions unanswered. Under fluoroscopy the cardiologist advances catheters through femoral vessels, recording pressures and saturations chamber by chamber. The same sitting can deliver balloons, coils, and occluder devices for treating the lesion found.
steps.tx: **Paediatric cardiac catheterisation** records chamber pressures and oxygen saturations directly through catheters placed under **fluoroscopy**, usually via **femoral venous and arterial** access. Diagnostic runs map shunts, stenoses, and resistances that echocardiography cannot resolve. Because balloons, coils, and **occluder devices** pass through the same catheters, diagnosis often converts to treatment in one sitting.

vis.caption: FFR assessment of LAD stenosis. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.say: Output cannot be guessed from pressures alone, so the laboratory applies the Fick principle. Oxygen consumption divided by the arteriovenous oxygen difference equals the blood flow across that circulation. The team measures consumption with a hood or assumes it, then samples saturations above and below the lungs.
steps.tx: The **Fick principle cardiac output** equals **oxygen consumption (VO2 in mL/min)** divided by the **arteriovenous oxygen difference (CaO2 minus CvO2)**. Higher consumption or a narrower extraction gap both raise the calculated flow. Accurate mixed venous and systemic arterial samples decide the result, so the catheter must sit free in the flowing stream and not wedged.

rows: Oxygen consumption in mL per minute
VO2 divided by CaO2 minus CvO2

steps.say: The commonest paediatric question is how big the shunt is. Pulmonary flow over systemic flow, written Qp by Qs, comes from four saturations: systemic arterial and mixed venous on top, pulmonary venous and pulmonary arterial below. A ratio above 1 means net left to right flow, and values near 2 usually earn closure.
steps.tx: The **shunt calculation formula** for the **Qp/Qs ratio** divides the systemic saturation gap by the pulmonary gap: **(systemic arterial sat minus mixed venous sat)** over **(pulmonary venous sat minus pulmonary arterial sat)**. A worked set of 98 and 70 above with 98 and 80 below gives 28 over 18, about **1.6 to 1**. Ratios above **2 to 1** with chamber enlargement generally indicate a shunt worth closing.

rows: 80 percent with a left to right shunt

steps.say: A sudden saturation jump between neighbouring chambers locates the hole. A rise of 7 to 8 percent or more from right atrium to right ventricle proves a ventricular level shunt, while a 9 to 10 percent rise from caval veins to right atrium proves an atrial level shunt. The catheter oximeter keeps mapping the step-up as it withdraws.
steps.tx: An **oximetric step-up** of **7-8% or more** between **right atrium and right ventricle** confirms a **left to right ventricular shunt** such as a VSD. A step-up of **9-10% or more** from **SVC or IVC to right atrium** confirms an **atrial shunt** such as an ASD. Serial samples during catheter withdrawal localise the defect level before angiography visualises it.

points: Rise of 7 to 8 percent from atrium to ventricle
left.title: Ventricular step-up

points: Rise of 9 to 10 percent from caval vein to atrium
right.title: Atrial step-up

steps.say: Pressures tell the second half of the story. Normal resting left ventricular end diastolic pressure in children is 6 to 12 millimetres of mercury, and values above 15 to 18 signal raised left sided filling pressures. Waveform shapes then separate tamponade, constriction, and restriction at the table.
steps.tx: Normal resting **left ventricular end diastolic pressure** in children is **6-12 mmHg**, while values above **15-18 mmHg** indicate elevated **left sided filling pressures**. End diastolic pressure guides diuretics, timing of valve surgery, and transplant listing. Characteristic **pressure waveforms** further separate tamponade equalisation from constrictive dip and plateau patterns.

vis.caption: Pericardial disease pressure patterns.

steps.say: Modern practice closes many defects without opening the chest. Ductal occlusion with Amplatzer duct occluders shuts suitable PDAs through a catheter, with balloon angioplasty opening native coarctation in older children plus recoarctation after surgery. Adolescents above 35 kilograms with coarctation usually receive covered stents instead.
steps.tx: **Transcatheter PDA closure** with **Amplatzer duct occluders** is standard for suitable ducts beyond infancy. **Balloon coarctation angioplasty** is the intervention of choice for **native coarctation** in older children and for **recoarctation** after surgery. **Covered stenting** is preferred in adolescents above **35 kg**, where recoil and wall injury make plain balloon dilatation less durable.

steps.say: Closing the wrong duct kills, so three situations forbid device closure. Active sepsis seeds any new hardware, severe pulmonary hypertension with a right to left shunt needs the duct as a pop-off, and duct dependent systemic lesions die if their lifeline shuts. Each of these is managed medically or surgically instead.
steps.tx: **Transcatheter PDA closure** is contraindicated with **active sepsis**, with **severe pulmonary hypertension and right to left shunt**, or with **duct dependent systemic lesions**. Sepsis guarantees device infection, a reversed shunt uses the duct as its only outlet, and a duct dependent circulation collapses without ductal flow. Such children need antibiotics, pulmonary vasodilators, prostaglandins, or surgery first.

steps.say: Children are not small adults for radiation or vessel injury. Femoral artery thrombosis strikes up to 3 to 5 percent of infants after arterial catheterisation and needs systemic heparinisation or tissue plasminogen activator. Dose control follows ALARA with pulsed fluoroscopy at three to seven and a half pulses per second, low dose detectors, and strict collimation.
steps.tx: **Vascular access complications** centre on **femoral artery thrombosis** in up to **3-5%** of infant arterial catheterisations, treated with systemic **heparinization** or **tissue plasminogen activator (tPA)**. Limb checks after every case catch a pale pulseless leg early. **Radiation dose reduction ALARA** uses **pulsed fluoroscopy at 3-7.5 pulses/second**, low dose detector settings, and strict **collimation** of the beam.
